analysis.title: US 2026 midterm elections: Election Day guide
key_insights: CACIB sees no last-minute shift in polling. The generic congressional ballot still favors Democrats in the House, and polls in many key Senate races lean Democratic.
CACIB's scenario odds: Democratic sweep 65%, Democratic House/Republican Senate 25%, Republican sweep 10%. Republican House/Democratic Senate is called highly unlikely.

In Michigan, Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers. CACIB does not expect it to swing the race since El-Sayed leads polls, but it adds uncertainty. A Republican flip in Michigan would narrow the Democratic path to the net four seats they need.
Legislative gridlock is the base case. The filibuster and a likely Trump veto mean a Democratic House with President Trump produces gridlock regardless of Senate control.

CACIB doubts a Democratic sweep would produce federal AI-buildout regulation, since Trump supports an aggressive buildout and would likely veto restrictions. Local politics (zoning limits on data centre construction) is the more likely constraint.

Trade and foreign policy are mostly executive-branch matters, so Congress offers little constraint. CACIB flags a behavioural risk: a heavy Republican defeat could prompt Trump to escalate in Iran or revive more aggressive tariffs.

Polls close from 18:00 EST (portions of IN and KY) to 1:00 EST Wednesday (Alaska Aleutians). Among key Senate states, SC closes at 19:00 EST, NC and OH at 19:30 EST. Exit polls show voter demographics and issues, not vote share.
Senate math: 35 seats are up (Republicans defend 22, Democrats 13). Republicans hold 53-47, so Democrats need a net gain of at least four seats, with VP Vance breaking a 50-50 tie.

Senate race buckets: North Carolina is a near-certain Democratic flip (watch the margin). MN and NH are Democrat-held and lean D. NE and SC are red states leaning R, where a tight race would signal a difficult night for Republicans. AK, IA, KS, ME, MI, OH and TX are the toss-ups, six held by Republicans and one by Democrats.

House math: Republicans hold 220-215, so Democrats need a net gain of at least three seats. Cook Political Report projects a Democratic net gain of 12-25 seats, with 18 toss-ups (14 Republican-held, four Democrat-held).

Timing of results is uncertain because of mail-in ballots, some accepted after Election Day if postmarked by it, and because close races take longer to call. A Senate call could come around midnight into Wednesday morning if Democrats do very well, or take days if control hinges on Alaska, which uses ranked-choice voting and accepts mail ballots until 18 November.

The House could be called late Tuesday if Democrats win decisively. Kentucky's 6th district (Trump +15 in 2024, now a toss-up, early poll close) is a bellwether. In a close result the call could take days. In 2022 the House was called on 16 November, eight days after Election Day, and California's mail-ballot rules could delay it.

Legal challenges are likely, especially in close races. The Trump administration has already challenged about 20k California mail-in ballots and tried to block Alaska from certifying a non-Sullivan winner, without success. CACIB does not expect challenges to succeed and expects a peaceful transition, with the new Congress sworn in on 3 January 2027.

tension_points.bull_case: Democrats are favoured in the Senate, with Polymarket giving roughly two-in-three odds. They have a near-certain flip in North Carolina and several realistic toss-up pickups, six of the seven toss-ups being Republican-held.
tension_points.bear_case: Democrats need a net gain of four seats from a 53-47 deficit. The Michigan seat, which Democrats hold, could flip after Stevens' endorsement of Rogers, and a toss-up like Alaska could leave control undecided for days.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Republicans flipping Michigan, or a tight race in Democrat-held MN or NH, would narrow the Democratic path.

theme_stances.key_argument: Democrats are favoured in the Senate, though to a lesser degree than in the House.
theme_stances.evidence: Democrats as a favourite in the Senate as well

theme_stances.key_argument: The filibuster and Trump's veto make gridlock the likely outcome regardless of Senate control.
